rows.design: open prospective study ([single arm, uncontrolled]; authors: 'Comparison with control and further follow up may add more information')
rows.body_site: shins 20%, forearms 14%, other sites in Table 2 (image, not in saved text); 'Most of the individuals had more than two sites of involvement'
rows.skin_tone: Fitzpatrick type IV 7 patients, type V 13 patients (Bangalore, India)
rows.patients_evaluable: 20 ('All the patients were reassessed at the end of 3 months')
rows.intervention: spot peel with 88% phenol, 0.5 ml applied with a cotton-tipped applicator over the whole macule plus 1 mm of normal skin, once a month for two sittings; topical 2% mupirocin twice daily for 7 to 10 days; daily sunlight exposure of 5 min after healing
rows.comparator: none (no control macules, no untreated arm)
rows.assessment_method: investigator five-point grading G0 to G4 (G0 no pigmentation, G1 up to 25%, G2 25-50%, G3 50-75%, G4 75% or more), with pretreatment photographs; patients' subjective response also recorded; blinding and number of assessors not reported
rows.time_from_start: 3 months ('at the end of 3 months of initiation of therapy')
rows.time_from_last_treatment: NOT_DERIVABLE: the paper times the assessment from initiation only ('at the end of 3 months of initiation of therapy'); [about 2 months] if the second sitting was exactly 1 month after the first ('The procedure was repeated after 1 month'), but actual session dates are not reported
rows.patient_noticeability: not reported (only 'The patient's subjective response correlated well with the investigators response'; no data given)
rows.complete_match: not reported (G4 is '75% or more pigmentation', not complete; Figure 1 shows one macule with 'Complete pigmentation' but no count is given)
rows.dark_overshoot: post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in 11.5% of pigmented lesions ([11.5% fits 16 of 139 treated macules, not any whole number of the 89 pigmented ones]); count only in Table 6 (image, not in saved text)
rows.texture_or_scar: persistent scabbing for more than 15 days in 17.2% of macules (abstract: 17.26%); ulceration, secondary infection and scarring also reported, counts only in Table 6 (image, not in saved text); 'common in elderly patients'
rows.attrition: none: 'All the patients were reassessed at the end of 3 months' (0 of 20 patients lost)
rows.citation: Ravikiran SP, Sacchidanand S, Leelavathy B. Therapeutic wounding - 88% phenol in idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis. Indian Dermatol Online J 2014;5(1):14-8
rows.source_location: Results, paragraph after Table 2; Abstract Results
rows.endpoint_definition: share of treated macules with any repigmentation at 3 months from initiation; partial repigmentation, not complete coverage
rows.uncertainty: [Uncontrolled single-arm study]; [about 7 macules per patient, 139/20,] analysed as independent. Patients were assessed after every session and finally at 3 months from initiation; no later follow-up (authors: 'further follow up may add more information'), so nothing on durability. Methods give age 20-85 years, Results give range 23-82 years. Co-interventions: daily 5-min sunlight after healing and topical mupirocin. Tables 1-6 are images and were not read; only numbers printed in the text are recorded. Blinding and number of assessors not reported. Scabbing is 17.26% in the Abstract vs 17.2% in Results. Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation 11.5% is said to be of 'pigmented lesions' but [fits 16/139, not n=89]. Methods list an unpaired t-test, Results use a paired t test for Table 3. How IGH was diagnosed (clinical, dermoscopy or biopsy) is not reported. Methods take 0.5 ml of phenol, Discussion says up to '1/2-1 ml in one session'. 'Repigmentation was noted in all the patients between 4 and 6 weeks', yet 50 macules had no response at 3 months (patient level vs macule level). The Introduction says the method 'is based on post inflammatory hyperpigmentation induced by chemical wounding', so the pigment seen at 3 months may be inflammatory pigment rather than a lasting colour match; with no later visit, durability is unknown. Figure 3 shows 'Perilesional spread of pigmentation', i.e. pigment beyond the macule edge (feathering covered 1 mm of normal skin), not a frequency. The Discussion asserts 'spontaneous repigmentation does not occur in any IGH lesions', but the study has no untreated control macules to show this.

verifier.notes: Verifier attempt 2, 2026-11-27: PASS, 0 failed cells. Checked both rows against papers/excerpts/ravikiran2014.txt alone (Europe PMC full text; Tables 1-6 are images). Every quote occurs in the source and supports its cell for the single phenol arm at 3 months from initiation. time_from_last_treatment NOT_DERIVABLE is right (assessment timed from initiation only; the bracketed ~2 months is marked as inference). analysis_unit is macules on both rows, row 1 denominator 89 stated. outcome_tier partial_repigmentation is the weakest reading on both rows (G4 is '75% or more'). Attrition and patients_evaluable now follow 'All the patients were reassessed at the end of 3 months'. Excess pigment (11.5%), scabbing (17.2%/17.26%), ulceration, infection and scarring recorded. Uncertainty now includes the post-inflammatory-hyperpigmentation mechanism. Observations, not failures: the Discussion calls the small sample size 'the only draw back' (n=20 is in the cells), and Methods exclude 'atrophic lesions' (an eligibility limit not named in uncertainty).
